title: If I Truly Learned From All of My Mistakes, I Would Be a Genius by Now
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles a common gap between the idea of 'failing forward' and what actually happens after a mistake: the lesson fades from memory long before it can be applied again. The author proposes a simple discipline: immediately writing down the takeaway from any misstep, and periodically reviewing the accumulated lessons rather than the failures themselves. Without this habit, the piece argues, leaders are destined to keep repeating avoidable mistakes because human memory alone can't be trusted to retain and surface hard-won wisdom at the right moment.
points: Popular culture embraces 'failing forward,' but lessons from mistakes often fade before they can be reapplied.
The author recommends immediately writing down the takeaway after any misstep.
Periodically reviewing accumulated lessons, not the failures themselves, keeps wisdom accessible.
Without this habit, leaders are likely to repeat the same mistakes over time.
Articulating a clear lesson is the test of whether a failure actually produced learning.
quotes: The idea of viewing mistakes and failures as opportunities to grow and as springboards to propel future success is now a part of popular culture.
After a few seasons, the learnings that were so powerful at the moment often fade away or are forgotten.
To extract the lessons and to keep them top of mind, good leaders follow a simple habit.
If you can’t articulate the lesson, takeaway, or action after a failure, you haven’t benefitted fully from it.
Wisdom from failure is how the best leaders own their responsibility for the future.
